clue.text: Blow recalling Norah Lofts's climber, perhaps

definitions.meaning: as a noun, blow is the flowering of a plant, as in 'roses in full blow'
Norah Lofts wrote the 1939 novel ... Like the Rose, and a rose is a climbing plant

explanation.surface: A blow that brings back a plant climbing through a novel by Norah Lofts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalling' is a link pointing to the Lofts title Blossom Like the Rose; 'climber, perhaps' is the rose itself, which the title says the answer is like.
explanation.definitionFit: Blow and bloom are old words for flowering, the same state the answer names.

clue.text: Comic relief, perhaps, on the part of theatre piece

parts.note: by can mean on the part of, as in 'a mistake by the referee'
a play is a piece written for the theatre

explanation.surface: A comic interlude is offered as part of a stage piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage business going on aside from the main action, such as a comic interlude, is the hyphenated term for side action.

definitions.meaning: Rosemary Sutcliff wrote the 1955 novel ... about a boy cast out of his tribe
rejected describes someone cast out by society, a pariah

explanation.surface: A subject treated by the writer Sutcliff is turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist is Rosemary Sutcliff; the extra E in the clue as held is presumably a misprint.
explanation.definitionFit: A pariah driven out of a community is one rejected, and Sutcliff's 1955 children's novel bears that title.

clue.text: What Sussex landscape painter will do, in confrontations?

definitions.text: What Sussex landscape painter will do
definitions.meaning: a painter of the Sussex landscape will exhibit pictures of the South Downs, the chalk hills of southern England
confrontations are decisive face-offs between opponents

explanation.surface: A painter of Sussex scenery is shown getting into fights.
explanation.walkthrough: The South Downs are chalk hills in Sussex, in southern England; the painter will display, or exhibit, pictures of those hills.
explanation.definitionFit: Final decisive clashes, as in a Western's gunfight at the end, are the plural noun for confrontations.

clue.text: Man of Argyle put out by king's half sister

indicators.note: put out suggests the letters are disturbed and thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A Scotsman from Argyll is upset by the monarch's half-sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' rearranges MAN OF ARGYLE into the enchantress's name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend the sorceress is the half-sister of King Arthur through their mother Igraine.

indicators.note: confuses means the letters of maestri are mixed into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone out hunting baffles the music masters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of the hunt is the archetypal huntress, a hunting type indeed.

parts.note: Bel is French for handsome, so the friend in the title is what was handsome

explanation.surface: A remark that something belonging to Maupassant was good-looking.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word for friend is the second half of the title Bel-Ami; 'bel', meaning handsome, is the first half.
explanation.definitionFit: In French a friend is called this, and Maupassant's title pairs that word with bel, handsome.

indicators.note: conceals means the word for a sibling hides the next piece inside it

parts.note: a twin is a sibling born at the same birth

explanation.surface: A brother or sister hides a writer of fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Twain, pen name of Samuel Clemens, wrote Huckleberry Finn and other novels.

indicators.note: hardly recognizable says the letters of in motet have been changed beyond recognition

explanation.surface: A composer can barely be made out within a choral motet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link but it is part of the fodder: IN plus MOTET give the seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gian Carlo Menotti was an Italian-American composer of operas such as Amahl and the Night Visitors.

clue.text: Some quiet contributions by Tillie Olsen

definitions.meaning: periods of quiet, more than one of them
Tillie Olsen's 1978 book of essays about writers kept from writing is titled ...

explanation.surface: A little quiet from the American writer Tillie Olsen.
explanation.definitionFit: Spells of stillness are plural quiets, and Olsen's essay collection about thwarted writers carries that plural title.

indicators.note: possibly signals that up to Prior could be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: An anthology which may be the work of the poet Matthew Prior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges UP TO PRIOR; Matthew Prior was an English poet, which makes 'up to' read like 'the responsibility of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A medley or mixed collection, such as an anthology of assorted pieces, is a miscellany.

clue.text: Parish record featured by John Galt

definitions.meaning: a year's record of events, here a parish chronicle
John Galt's 1821 novel is ... of the Parish, so a single such record is featured in his title

explanation.surface: A church register appears in a book by the Scottish novelist John Galt.
explanation.definitionFit: A single year's entry in a chronicle is the singular of the word for historical records.

clue.text: A drawback, but not for a struggling writer

indicators.note: back tells us the word draw in the clue is read from right to left

explanation.surface: A drawback, but not one that afflicts an impoverished author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawback' is split: 'back' turns the word draw. The definition is wry: prizes go to the successful, seldom to the strugglers who need them.
explanation.definitionFit: A prize such as a literary grant is given to writers who have succeeded, ironically rarely the strugglers.

parts.note: Trollope's novel The Small House at ... names a modest home and the village where it stands

explanation.surface: Asking where the novelist Trollope's little house was.
explanation.definitionFit: The village in Trollope's Barsetshire novel The Small House at Allington is where that small house stands.

clue.text: Mere feature near hellhole in Campania

definitions.text: Mere feature near hellhole in Campania

parts.words: Mere feature near hellhole in Campania
parts.note: a mere is a lake, and this volcanic crater lake near Naples was held by the Romans to be the entrance to the underworld

explanation.surface: A pond near a squalid dive in southern Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hellhole' sounds like a squalid place, but the Romans literally believed this crater led down to Hades; Campania is the region round Naples.
explanation.definitionFit: The crater lake near Cumae was thought by the ancients to be a gateway to the underworld.

definitions.meaning: Nevil Shute's 1950 novel is titled after an Australian outback settlement
Dodgson, writing as Lewis Carroll, created Alice, so a settlement resembling her would be described this way

explanation.surface: Nevil Shute's setting is compared to Lewis Carroll's heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: The title refers to Alice Springs in Australia; the clue playfully reads it as a town resembling Carroll's Alice.
explanation.definitionFit: Shute named his novel for Alice Springs, and taken literally the title compares a settlement to Carroll's heroine.

clue.text: Inaccurately cite haste to describe an attitude of Pre-Raphaelite

indicators.note: inaccurately means cite haste is set down wrongly, its letters out of order

explanation.surface: Quoting hastily and wrongly to sum up the outlook of a Pre-Raphaelite painter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pre-Raphaelites fed into the Aesthetic movement, whose creed of art for art's sake is this outlook.

definitions.meaning: a pale yellow flower of early spring
The clergyman in Goldsmith's The Vicar of Wakefield, Wakefield being a town in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A spring flower given to a clergyman from Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The churchman is Goldsmith's Vicar of Wakefield, Dr Primrose; Wakefield is in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: This pale yellow flower blooms in early spring, and it is also the surname of Goldsmith's vicar.

definitions.meaning: William Golding's 1980 Booker-winning novel set on a ship bears this title
ceremonies held only in a passage or corridor, taking the phrase literally

explanation.surface: A Golding ritual held only in the hallway.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally, rites held in a passage, or lobby; normally the phrase means ceremonies marking a stage of life.
explanation.definitionFit: Golding's sea novel shares its title with the ceremonies that mark a life change, here wittily held in a corridor.

indicators.note: flop suggests the letters of theatre collapse and land in a different order

explanation.surface: A theatrical failure happens there.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb meaning there, at that spot, as in 'he was angered thereat'.

clue.text: Eldest daughter left on Rhode Island with a pound

parts.note: RI is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Rhode Island
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A firstborn daughter heads off to Rhode Island carrying a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: In King Lear, Goneril is the first of the king's three daughters.

parts.note: the Scottish poet G S ... published a collection called Conditions in 1969

explanation.surface: A poet who laid down terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made conditions' reads as setting terms, but it means wrote the poetry book Conditions.
explanation.definitionFit: G S Fraser was a Scottish poet and critic whose collection bears the title Conditions.

clue.text: Mother of nine (doubtless had a way of remembering their names)

definitions.meaning: in Greek myth she bore Zeus the nine Muses

definitions.text: doubtless had a way of remembering their names
definitions.meaning: she is the goddess of memory, so she would have no trouble recalling her children's names

explanation.surface: A mother of nine children surely had a trick for keeping their names straight.
explanation.walkthrough: Her name is the root of mnemonic, a device for remembering.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titaness of memory bore the nine Muses to Zeus.

clue.text: Quantity of civet required to sweeten Lear's imagination

definitions.text: Quantity of civet required to sweeten Lear's imagination

parts.words: Quantity of civet required to sweeten Lear's imagination
parts.note: Lear says 'Give me an ... of civet, good apothecary, to sweeten my imagination', asking for a small weight of perfume

explanation.surface: A measure of perfume that King Lear wanted to purify his thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: Civet is a musky perfume; the line comes from King Lear, Act 4, Scene 6.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear asks the apothecary for a small weight of civet, one sixteenth of a pound.

definitions.meaning: a distinction or award, spelt without the u in the US
Anna Maria Porter's 1826 novel is titled with this heroine's name followed by O'Hara

explanation.surface: Is a US award due to the O'Hara of a writer named Porter?
explanation.walkthrough: The Porter is Anna Maria Porter, not Cole or Katherine Anne; 'American' signals the spelling without U.
explanation.definitionFit: An accolade is a distinction or tribute, spelt in the US style, and it is also the first name of Porter's heroine.

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: A poem about the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The cinema chain name derives from the Greek building for music performances, a theatre.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Heard Waughlike title 2, (3,2,4)', is garbled by OCR: 'Heard' and the stray '2,' leave no sound parse beyond the Waugh novel title Men at Arms.

clue.text: Encountered leading minimalist enter ing Tate

indicators.note: leading takes the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Met the foremost minimalist at the Tate gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text splits 'entering' into 'enter ing'; its first letter is still E, so 'leading' gives M, E and T.
explanation.definitionFit: To have come across someone is to have encountered them, the past tense of the verb.

clue.text: "He did me, past all saying nay" (Merchant of Venice)

definitions.text: "He did me, past all saying nay" (Merchant of Venice)

parts.words: He did me, past all saying nay
parts.note: the line from The Merchant of Venice has a word missing between did and me, meaning implored

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice with a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Portia's line about Bassanio's ring: 'He did ... me, past all saying nay'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means begged or implored, which completes the Shakespeare line.

parts.note: Horace's Carmen Saeculare is a hymn for the centennial games; the Latin adjective has an English form

explanation.surface: An English rendering of a song by Horace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carmen' is not Bizet's opera but Latin for song; Horace wrote the Carmen Saeculare.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin saeculare, of an age or century, gives the English word meaning worldly, not religious.
